# The AI-readiness proof

*Stage 6 artifact. Owner: Aaron Robbins. Generated by
`src/stage6_ai_readiness.py` from the frozen snapshot. Regenerate it;
never hand-edit it.*

One legal-operations question, answered twice.

> **How long does it take to resolve a contract dispute in federal
> court?**

| | Answer |
|---|---|
| Against the raw frozen file | **-742.3 days** |
| Against the governed model | **208.0 days** |

Both numbers come from the same 2.0 GB file, retrieved once, on the
same day. Neither query contains a mistake anyone would call obvious.

---

## The ungoverned answer is not approximately right

It is **-742.3 days**, and 32,767 of the matters behind it have a *negative*
duration -- some of them by more than a century. The arithmetic is
correct. Every input is a well-formed date. Nothing errors, nothing
warns, and no null appears anywhere to hint that something is wrong.

**That is the whole argument.** A governed layer is not documentation
wrapped around a correct answer. It is the difference between an answer
and a number.

## The decomposition

Each row is one governance rule earning its place. The query is the
same query throughout; only the rules change.

| # | Step | Records | Answer, days | Why | Rule |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| 0 | the obvious query, reader defaults | 1,413,149 | -742.3 | nothing corrected yet | - |
| 1 | + correct the encoding | 1,413,149 | -742.3 (+0.0) | the file is not UTF-8 (measured: zero rows recovered) | CLAUDE.md source property 1 |
| 2 | + disable quoting | 1,413,149 | -742.3 (-0.0) | no quoting convention; party names contain bare quotes | CLAUDE.md source property 2 |
| 3 | + quarantine field-shifted records | 1,413,138 | -742.3 (+0.0) | 638 records carry a tab inside the defendant name | docket-to-matter.md R-04 |
| 4 | + exclude pending matters | 1,380,371 | 319.8 (+1062.0) | pending records carry TERMDATE = 01/01/1900, not null | source-register.md F-02 |
| 5 | + one record per matter (reopenings) | 1,378,578 | 319.6 (-0.1) | a reopened matter produces a second status record | docket-to-matter.md R-01.b |
| 6 | + the subject-matter control | 1,370,419 | 319.5 (-0.1) | carrier parties excluded at docket level | subject-matter-filter.md |
| 7 | + median, not mean | 1,370,419 | 208.0 (-111.5) | litigation durations are heavily right-skewed | metric_register.md M-01 |

**Step 4 does all the work, and steps 1 to 3 do almost none.** That is
the honest reading of this table and it is not the one the exercise was
set up to produce. The encoding and the quoting are real defects in the
source and they cost 11 records here, not thousands. One rule out of
seven moves the answer by 1,062 days; the rest move it by less than a
day between them, until the mean-versus-median choice at step 7.

The reason to keep steps 1 to 3 anyway is that **their cost is not
bounded by this measure.** The 638 field-shifted records carry
disposition codes that are fragments of dates, and they will corrupt
M-02 and M-03 rather than M-01. A rule is not worthless because the
first question you ask happens not to depend on it.

## Step 1 cost nothing here, and that is worth stating plainly

The file is not UTF-8. A reader at its defaults raises an error, and
the error message suggests `ignore_errors=true`. Taking that advice
makes the error go away.

**It also lost nothing.** Both readings return 10,960,173 records; the
recovery is exactly zero rows. An earlier draft of this document
asserted that the suppression discarded records. It was checked, and it
did not, and the sentence was removed rather than softened.

The hazard is still real and is narrower than it first looked:
`ignore_errors=true` suppresses an *unbounded* number of failures and
reports none of them. Here the number happened to be zero, and nothing
in the output said so. The analyst who follows the tool's advice cannot
distinguish that case from the one where it drops a hundred thousand
rows. That is why this module counts records at every stage and writes
the counts to `governance/last_run.json` -- not because suppression is
always lossy, but because unmeasured suppression is never assertable.

## There is no obvious correct filter

Suppose the analyst *does* notice the pending records and reaches for
the obvious fix -- keep only rows the source marks as terminated:

```sql
WHERE STATUSCD = 'L'
```

That gives **332.3 days** over 776,020 records -- and quietly discards every
matter before statistical year 2001, because `STATUSCD` did not exist
then. The careful analyst loses 637,118 records -- 44 percent of the slice --
and gets a different wrong answer than the careless one, biased toward
recent years.

**Both reasonable choices are wrong, in opposite directions.** Only an
effective-dated closure rule is right, and that rule is not derivable
from the data -- it comes from a sentence in the codebook stating that
the field was captured from October 2000. That sentence is why
`docket-to-matter.md` R-03 exists.

## What this means for an AI layer

A retrieval system pointed at the raw file answers the question with
**-742.3 days**, fluently and with a citation to a real government
dataset. It has no way to know about the sentinel date, because the
sentinel is not written down anywhere in the file -- it is written down
in this repository, in a governance document, by a person who found it
and took ownership of it.

Governance is not the paperwork that slows the AI layer down. It is the
only thing standing between a fluent answer and a correct one. That is
what *governed, well-modeled enterprise data supports AI* has to mean
if it means anything.

## The trend agrees, and the reason it agrees is an accident

Plotted by statistical year, 2001 to 2025:

| | First year | Last year | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Ungoverned, mean days | 285.1 | 362.0 | +77.0 |
| Governed, median days | 174.0 | 263.0 | +89.0 |

**Both paths agree that contract matters are getting slower**, by a
broadly similar amount. The ungoverned line is offset by roughly 111
days -- that offset is the mean-versus-median choice, not the sentinel.

This is not the result the exercise wanted, and it is the most useful
one in the document.

**The trend chart is clean because the defect hides from it.** Pending
records carry `TAPEYEAR = 2099`. Group by year and all 32,767 of them
fall into a bucket that is off the end of every axis anyone would draw.
The chart never shows them. The headline average, which has no year
axis to hide behind, is wrong by more than a thousand days.

So the same defect, in the same file, on the same day, is **invisible
in one cut of the data and catastrophic in another.** An analyst who
sanity-checks the headline against the trend chart finds a plausible
line going the right way and concludes the number is fine.

That is the case for a governed layer stated more precisely than
"ungoverned answers are wrong." Ungoverned answers are wrong
*inconsistently*, and inconsistent wrongness is what defeats review.
You cannot eyeball your way out of it, because the cut of the data you
would eyeball is the one that looks right.
